basics: The respiratory system is a set of tubes and sacs that brings outside air close enough to blood for gases to diffuse across a thin wall. The slide gives two different ways to cut the system in two. Anatomically, 'upper' means everything in the head and neck down to (but not including) the larynx: nose, nasal cavity and pharynx; 'lower' is larynx, trachea, bronchi and lungs. Note the slide's line 'nostrils to larynx' is ambiguous: Tortora puts the larynx in the lower tract. Functionally, the 'conducting' part (nose to terminal bronchioles) only moves, cleans, warms and humidifies air, with no gas exchange; the 'respiratory' part (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli) is where oxygen and carbon dioxide actually cross into and out of blood. The two classifications overlap but do not coincide: much of the conducting zone lies inside the lungs, i.e. in the lower tract.

basics: Cells burn fuel with oxygen and produce carbon dioxide; the respiratory system's core job is to keep the blood's O2 up and CO2 down by exchanging both with the atmosphere. Everything else on the slide is a side-effect of moving air or of having an enormous blood-perfused surface. Sound: air pushed past the vocal folds makes them vibrate, and the nose, sinuses and mouth shape the sound. Smell: receptors sit in the roof of the nasal cavity, so odour molecules in inhaled air reach them. Acid–base: CO2 dissolved in water forms carbonic acid, so breathing more or less CO2 out raises or lowers blood pH within minutes. Blood pressure: the lung capillaries carry an enzyme (ACE) that converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II, a hormone that constricts vessels and makes the kidney keep salt and water. The slide does not mention two further items in the book: excretion of water and heat in exhaled air, and filtering of inspired air.

basics: The visible nose is a scaffold, not a solid organ. Its upper third is bone (the two nasal bones plus parts of the frontal bone and maxillae), and its lower two-thirds is hyaline cartilage: a central septal cartilage forming the front of the partition between the two nostrils, a pair of lateral cartilages below the nasal bones, and the alar cartilages (major and minor) that curve round to form the nostril walls. The 'ala' (wing) is the soft flared side of the nostril, which in the figure is mostly dense connective and fatty tissue rather than cartilage. Cartilage is bendable, which is why the tip of the nose can be pushed sideways without breaking. The slide's three verbs (warm, filter, humidify) describe what happens once air is inside: coarse hairs at the entrance catch large particles, and the moist, blood-rich lining behind them heats and wets the air before it reaches the delicate lung tissue.

basics: A median (mid-line) section cuts the head into left and right halves, so you see the air route in profile. The septum labels on the slide show that the nasal partition is cartilage in front and two bones behind: the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above and the vomer below.

basics: The larynx is a short box of cartilage plates hinged together by ligaments and small muscles, sitting at the top of the trachea in front of vertebrae C4–C6. Its job is to keep the airway open while still being able to seal it (during swallowing or straining) and to hold the vocal folds under adjustable tension. Nine cartilages: three single (the big shield-shaped thyroid cartilage in front, whose forward ridge is the 'Adam's apple'; the ring-shaped cricoid at the bottom; the leaf-shaped elastic epiglottis on top) and three pairs (arytenoids, which pivot on the back of the cricoid and pull the vocal folds; corniculates on the arytenoid tips; cuneiforms in the fold in front of them). The hyoid bone above is not part of the larynx but suspends it. When you swallow, muscles lift the larynx; the tongue base pushes the epiglottis down over the opening, so food slides into the oesophagus behind.

basics: Sound is a vibration of air. The vocal folds are two shelves of tissue stretched from the thyroid cartilage in front to the two arytenoid cartilages behind; the gap between them is the rima glottidis. Because the arytenoids can rotate on the cricoid, small muscles can swing the folds apart or together. Posterior cricoarytenoid muscles rotate the arytenoids outward and open the gap (abduction) so air passes silently; lateral cricoarytenoids rotate them inward and close the gap (adduction). With the folds nearly closed, air pushed up from the lungs forces them apart in rapid pulses and they snap back elastically, chopping the airflow into pressure waves: that is voice. Pitch depends on fold tension (tighter = faster vibration = higher note); loudness on air pressure. The slide does not say that the pharynx, mouth and nose then shape this buzz into recognisable vowels and words.

basics: The trachea is a 12 cm, 2.5 cm-wide tube kept open by 16–20 C-shaped hoops of hyaline cartilage stacked like a vacuum-cleaner hose. The open back of each C faces the oesophagus and is bridged by smooth muscle (trachealis), so a swallowed lump can bulge forwards without hitting rigid cartilage. Rigid support matters because inhalation creates suction that would otherwise collapse a soft tube. The inner lining is 'respiratory epithelium': tall ciliated cells with scattered goblet cells that secrete mucus. Particles stick to the mucus, and the cilia beat in a coordinated wave that carries the sheet upward to the pharynx to be swallowed (the mucociliary escalator). At the level of the T4/T5 vertebral junction the trachea forks into right and left main bronchi at an internal ridge, the carina. The slide's histology panel shows the same layers seen in cross-section: mucosa, submucosal mucous glands, the cartilage ring with its chondrocytes and perichondrium.

basics: Below the carina the airway tree branches repeatedly, and each branch level has a name tied to the anatomy it serves. The two main (primary) bronchi go one to each lung; the right one is wider, shorter and more vertical, which is why inhaled objects usually end up on the right. Each main bronchus splits into lobar (secondary) bronchi, one per lobe: three on the right (superior, middle, inferior), two on the left. Lobar bronchi split into segmental (tertiary) bronchi, each supplying a wedge of lung called a bronchopulmonary segment, a unit a surgeon can remove on its own. The slide's label 'segmental bronchi of middle lobe' is simply the tertiary branches inside the right middle lobe. Like the trachea, the main bronchi still have C-rings of cartilage and a ciliated mucous lining; the cartilage becomes plates and then vanishes as the tubes narrow.

basics: Counting 'generations' is a way of describing a tree: each time a tube splits, its daughters are one generation higher. Trachea = 0, main bronchi = 1, and so on for roughly 23 splits until the blind-ended alveolar sacs. Because each split doubles the number of tubes, by generation 23 there are millions of tiny passages, and their combined wall area is enormous (Tortora estimates 300–500 million alveoli, about 75 square metres). Generations up to the terminal bronchioles (about 16) are conducting only; from the respiratory bronchioles onward (about 17–23) alveoli bud from the walls and gas exchange begins. As tubes narrow, the tall ciliated lining becomes low cuboidal then flat squamous, cartilage disappears and smooth muscle takes over, which is why bronchioles can constrict in asthma. The sponge-like feel of a lung is simply this froth of thin-walled sacs.

basics: A lung lobule is the smallest self-contained unit: one terminal bronchiole enters it with a small artery, and a small vein and lymphatic leave it, all wrapped in elastic connective tissue. Inside, the bronchiole becomes respiratory bronchioles, then alveolar ducts, ending in grape-like alveolar sacs. The arteriole breaks up into a dense capillary mesh draped over every alveolus like a net over a balloon, then re-collects into the venule. Crucially the arteriole is a branch of the pulmonary artery, which carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle; the venule feeds the pulmonary veins, which carry freshly oxygenated blood to the left atrium. So in the lung the naming is reversed relative to the rest of the body: arteries carry 'blue' blood, veins 'red'. The slide omits the second, small blood supply (bronchial arteries from the aorta) that feeds the airway walls themselves.

basics: An alveolus is a bubble about a quarter of a millimetre across whose wall is a single layer of epithelium on a basement membrane, with capillaries pressed against the outside. Two epithelial cell types form the wall. Type I cells (the slide's 'squamous alveolar cells') are extremely flattened and cover about 95% of the surface; being thin is their whole function, because diffusion time scales with the square of distance. Type II cells (the slide's 'great' cells, Tortora's septal cells) are cuboidal, sit between the type I cells, secrete the watery lining fluid and its surfactant, and act as stem cells that divide to replace damaged type I cells. Surfactant is a detergent-like mix of phospholipids and proteins that lowers the surface tension of the water film so small alveoli do not collapse. Alveolar macrophages are wandering white cells that crawl over the surface eating dust and bacteria that slipped past the mucus of the airways. The slide's 'lymphocyte' is another immune cell in the wall.

basics: For a gas molecule to go from alveolar air into a red cell it must cross, in order: the surfactant-lined fluid film, the flat type I cell, the epithelial basement membrane, the capillary basement membrane (usually fused with the previous one), and the capillary endothelial cell, then the plasma and the red cell membrane. Tortora counts four tissue layers and quotes a total thickness of about 0.5 micrometres, one-sixteenth of a red cell's diameter. Gas crosses purely by diffusion, driven by partial-pressure differences; no pump is involved, so thinness and area are everything. The slide's 'alveolar pores' are small holes between neighbouring alveoli that equalise pressure and give collateral air routes. A red blood cell is a biconcave disc with no nucleus or mitochondria, which maximises room for haemoglobin and gives a large surface-to-volume ratio for fast gas loading; the cells pass the capillaries in single file, so the diffusion path inside blood is short too.

basics: Pressure difference drives airflow, but three properties set how much flow a given pressure buys. (1) Surface tension: every alveolus is lined by water, and the inward pull of that film acts like a tiny balloon trying to shrink; by Laplace's law smaller bubbles have higher collapsing pressure, so without help the small alveoli would empty into big ones. Surfactant, a phospholipid film from type II cells, cuts the surface tension and does so more in smaller alveoli, stabilising them; premature babies lacking it develop respiratory distress syndrome. (2) Compliance: the change in volume per unit change in pressure, i.e. how easily the lung and chest wall stretch; scarring, fluid or surfactant deficiency lower it (stiff lungs), emphysema raises it (floppy lungs that do not recoil). (3) Airway resistance: like resistance in a pipe, dominated by the diameter of the bronchioles, which the sympathetic nerves widen and the parasympathetic nerves or histamine narrow; asthma and COPD are diseases of raised resistance.

terms.d: Volume change per unit pressure change; high compliance = easy to inflate.

basics: 'Respiration' in physiology is a chain of three transport steps plus a chemical one. Step 1, ventilation, moves air by bulk flow between atmosphere and alveoli. Step 2, external respiration, is diffusion across the alveolar wall: O2 into pulmonary capillary blood, CO2 out. The blood then carries the gases around the body (transport, not usually numbered as a step). Step 3, internal respiration, is diffusion at the tissue capillaries: O2 out to cells, CO2 in. Inside the cells, cellular respiration is the metabolic burning of fuel with O2 to make ATP, releasing CO2; that is the reason the other steps exist. Keeping the terms apart avoids a common confusion: 'external' does not mean outside the body but exchange with the external air at the lungs.

basics: Haemoglobin is a protein of four sub-units (two alpha and two beta chains), each folded around a flat ring molecule called heme with a single iron atom in its centre. The iron, in its Fe2+ state, can bind one O2 molecule loosely and reversibly, so each haemoglobin carries up to four O2. The binding is cooperative: when one heme takes up oxygen the protein's shape shifts slightly and the other hemes bind more easily, which produces the S-shaped saturation curve on the next slides. The 'crystal structure' in the title refers to how the picture was obtained: X-ray diffraction of haemoglobin crystals, the ribbons being the polypeptide backbones. Each red cell holds about 280 million of these molecules, roughly a third of the cell's weight, which is why oxygen is carried almost entirely inside red cells rather than dissolved.

basics: Plot the fraction of haemoglobin's four sites that hold O2 against the PO2 of the surrounding plasma and you get an S-shaped curve, not a straight line, because of cooperative binding. The steep part (PO2 20–40 mmHg) is where tissue capillaries operate, so small drops in tissue PO2 release large amounts of O2; the flat plateau (60–100 mmHg) is where the lungs operate, so haemoglobin loads fully even if alveolar PO2 falls somewhat (altitude, mild lung disease). At the normal arterial PO2 of ~100 mmHg it is about 97–98% saturated; at the resting venous PO2 of 40 it is still about 75%, meaning resting tissues take only a quarter of the load; at 20 mmHg only about 35% remains. 'Saturation' is a percentage of capacity, not an amount: total O2 carried also depends on how much haemoglobin the blood contains.

basics: By Henry's law, plasma at a PO2 of 100 mmHg dissolves only about 0.3 mL of O2 per 100 mL, far too little to run a body that needs about 250 mL per minute at rest. Haemoglobin solves this by binding O2 chemically without raising its partial pressure, so that 100 mL of arterial blood carries about 20 mL of O2, of which roughly 98.5% (the slide says >98%) is on haemoglobin and 1.5% is dissolved. The two pools interact: only dissolved O2 can diffuse out into tissues, and as it leaves, the falling plasma PO2 makes haemoglobin release more, which re-dissolves and follows. The dissolved fraction therefore sets the PO2 you measure, while the bound fraction is the reservoir. This is why anaemia (less haemoglobin) lowers O2 content without changing arterial PO2.

basics: CO2 made by cells diffuses into capillary blood and is handled three ways. About 7% simply dissolves (CO2 is 24 times more soluble than O2). About 23% attaches to amino groups on proteins, mostly haemoglobin, as carbaminohaemoglobin, and deoxygenated Hb binds CO2 more readily (Haldane effect). About 70% is converted inside red cells: carbonic anhydrase, an enzyme absent from plasma, joins CO2 and water into carbonic acid, which splits into H+ and bicarbonate. Bicarbonate leaves the cell into plasma, and to keep charge balance a chloride ion moves in (the chloride shift). The H+ is buffered by haemoglobin; binding H+ nudges haemoglobin into a shape that holds O2 less tightly, so O2 unloads exactly where CO2 is being produced (Bohr effect). The slide's line that H+ 'creates a local change in pH' is this buffering: most H+ never reaches the plasma.

basics: Everything on the previous slide runs backwards in the lung because the driving gradients flip. basics: 'Shifting right' means that at any given PO2 haemoglobin holds less O2, i.e. its affinity has fallen, so more O2 is released to tissues; shifting left means the opposite. Four factors shift it right, and all four are signs of a hard-working tissue: more CO2, more H+ (lower pH), higher temperature, and more 2,3-BPG. CO2 and H+ act through the Bohr effect: H+ binding to the globin chains changes the protein's shape so the hemes let go of O2. BPG is a by-product of glycolysis in red cells that wedges between the beta chains and stabilises the low-affinity form; it rises within hours in hypoxia, at altitude, and under hormones such as thyroxine and adrenaline. The lecturer's phrase 'right and downward' describes the same shift. In the lungs the reverse conditions (CO2 leaving, pH rising, cooler) shift the curve left and help loading. Fetal haemoglobin sits to the left because it binds BPG weakly.

basics: Breathing muscles are skeletal muscles, so they contract only when nerves tell them to; the rhythm comes from clusters of neurons in the brainstem, collectively the respiratory centre. In the medulla, the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) fires in ~2-second bursts to the diaphragm (via the phrenic nerves) and the external intercostals, producing quiet inhalation; when it stops, exhalation happens by recoil. A group in the pons (pontine respiratory group) fine-tunes the rhythm. The lecturer's 'pneumotaxic' and 'apneustic' centres are older names for pontine regions: Tortora calls the first the pontine respiratory group and no longer describes an apneustic centre. Chemical signals (CO2/H+) reach these groups from chemoreceptors via cranial nerves IX and X, and the cortex, hypothalamus and limbic system can override or colour the rhythm (speech, breath-holding, emotion).

basics: A chemoreceptor is a neuron whose firing rate depends on the concentration of a chemical. basics: Peripheral chemoreceptors are small blood-rich nodules outside the brain: the carotid bodies at the fork of each common carotid artery (signalling through the glossopharyngeal nerve, IX) and the aortic bodies on the aortic arch (signalling through the vagus, X). basics: Read the flowchart as a thermostat. The controlled variable is really arterial PCO2 (with pH and PO2 as secondary inputs). A disturbance, say exercise producing extra CO2 and acid, raises arterial PCO2 and H+ and lowers PO2. Peripheral chemoreceptors read the blood directly; central chemoreceptors read CO2 that has diffused into brain fluid and turned into H+. Both increase their firing to the medullary inspiratory neurons (the DRG), which fire harder and more often down the phrenic and intercostal nerves; diaphragm and intercostals contract more strongly and quickly; ventilation rises; more CO2 is exhaled and more O2 taken up; the blood values return toward normal and the receptor drive fades. The effect is opposite in sign to the disturbance, hence negative feedback. Note the asymmetry the slide omits: the system is far more sensitive to a rise in CO2 than to a fall in O2.

basics: Beyond chemistry, three kinds of mechanical or irritant input adjust breathing. Irritant receptors are bare nerve endings in the airway epithelium; dust, smoke, pollen or cold air trigger them and the reflex output is a cough or sneeze (a brief pause, deep inhalation, glottis closure, explosive exhalation), plus reflex narrowing of the bronchi and shallow rapid breathing, all aimed at keeping the irritant out of the alveoli. Proprioceptors in muscles, tendons and joints report body movement; the moment you start to exercise they excite the DRG, which is why ventilation rises before any change in blood gases. Stretch receptors in the smooth muscle of bronchi and bronchioles (the slide adds the visceral pleura) signal through the vagus to inhibit the DRG when the lung is over-inflated. Tortora treats irritation under 'Other influences on breathing' and does not name 'irritant receptors' as a receptor class.

terms.d: Free nerve endings in airway lining that respond to particles, chemicals or cold and provoke cough or bronchoconstriction.
